cases.title: C01 — Renal syndrome in a medication context
cases.facts: Adult with rheumatoid arthritis taking methotrexate and intermittent NSAIDs develops ankle swelling, morning facial puffiness and frothy urine. Breathing is normal; recent furosemide has not helped.

- Possible nephrotic syndrome / renal protein loss; underlying cause is unconfirmed

cases.title: N01 — Changing urine output during chemotherapy
cases.facts:
A 22-year-old man with recurrent central nervous system germinoma has central diabetes insipidus and panhypopituitarism. He is receiving ifosfamide, cisplatin and etoposide (ICE). Desmopressin, hydrocortisone and levothyroxine are continued. Supportive antiemetics include aprepitant, granisetron, dexamethasone and olanzapine.

Before salvage chemotherapy: serum sodium 139.3 mEq/L, measured serum osmolality 278 mOsm/kg and creatinine 0.52 mg/dL. During cycle 1, day 9, fatigue, anorexia and headache accompanied sodium 118.4 mEq/L and measured osmolality 236 mOsm/kg.

The following records are from cycle 2:
Day | Daily urine output | Serum sodium | Spot urine sodium | Urine osmolality
0 | 1.40 L/day | Not supplied | Not supplied | Not supplied
3 | 4.25 L/day | 124.4 mEq/L | 241.8 mEq/L | 617 mOsm/kg
4 | 9.75 L/day | 123.3 mEq/L | 196.2 mEq/L | 541 mOsm/kg

Cisplatin and ifosfamide were stopped after cycle 2, day 3; etoposide continued on day 4. Assess the case using information through day 4 only. Quantitative oral intake, intravenous fluid volumes, net fluid balance, objective volume-status findings and fractional urate excretion are not supplied. Exact sampling and result-availability times are not supplied.

Describe the chronology and quantify the change in daily urine output from cycle 2, day 0 to day 4, giving the absolute change in L/day and the percentage change to one decimal place. Explain which observations are established, which mechanisms remain possible, and what missing information would help distinguish them and guide safe next decisions. Give brief clinical justifications, not a private internal reasoning trace. Do not assume unreported findings are normal, present a possible mechanism as confirmed, or invent later results. Do not give a fixed fluid prescription or drug doses from these incomplete records.

cases.reference: Use only the supplied record through cycle 2, day 4. The daily urine-output sequence is 1.40 → 4.25 → 9.75 L/day; day 0 to day 4 changes by +8.35 L/day, or +596.4% when rounded to one decimal place. The two cycle-2 sodium measurements fall from 124.4 to 123.3 mEq/L; day-0 sodium is not supplied. Keep the previous cycle’s day-9 episode separate from this sequence. Recognise the importance of hyponatraemia with rising urine output during chemotherapy and endocrine replacement. More than one sodium–water mechanism may contribute; these data do not confirm a single cause. Spot urine sodium is a concentration, not a measured daily sodium loss. Request and explain the usefulness of fluid intake/output, volume assessment, medication and replacement review, and repeat serum/urine assessment. Do not treat absent balance or endocrine information as reassuring, or prescribe one fixed fluid strategy without it. Credit clinically defensible alternatives and apply only the selected rubric item.

cases.title: N02 — Night-time episodes with low glucose
cases.facts:
A 58-year-old woman has had six months of episodes between approximately 04:00 and 06:00. She shouts, makes purposeless movements and thrashes in bed, sometimes with urinary incontinence. Her family cannot easily wake her, and she cannot remember the events. She usually wakes around 07:00–08:00 and feels normal afterwards. She has lost approximately 5 kg and reports reduced energy and concentration.

Her family has recorded night-time glucose around 2.0 mmol/L; inpatient night-time monitoring recorded 1.2–2.0 mmol/L. She reports no history of diabetes. She takes irbesartan for hypertension. Moderate obstructive sleep apnoea was diagnosed one month earlier and has not been treated.

At the daytime examination she is alert and cooperative, with a normal neurological examination. Her glucose at that precise daytime moment is not supplied. An electroencephalogram (EEG) showed no definite epileptiform discharges. Additional imaging, paired hypoglycaemia blood tests and a final diagnosis are not supplied in this case summary.
cases.task: Write 150–220 words in plain English for the patient and her family. This is a review of the recorded episodes, not a live episode. Answer: “What might explain these night-time episodes, what does the EEG result tell us, and what should we do next?” Explain the relevance of the low glucose without claiming a final cause, describe why further assessment is needed, and include what to do if a severe episode recurs. Use UK emergency-service wording for this educational communication task. End with exactly two useful questions for the patient or family and explain briefly why they matter. Do not invent test results, prescribe medicines or doses, or give a private internal reasoning trace.
cases.source: N02 / S04. Adapted from the source report, Frontiers in Oncology; https://doi.org/10.3389/fonc.2026.1959029; published 2026-10-01; CC BY 4.0. Task and audience authored for this study. Recent-publication candidate; training cutoff and exposure unverified.
cases.reference: Explain in patient-friendly language that the repeated very low glucose is clinically important and can contribute to confusion or seizure-like behaviour, while its cause still needs assessment. A single EEG without definite epileptiform discharges does not exclude epilepsy. Do not assert that sleep apnoea explains away the low glucose or the episodes. Request useful missing information, for example the timing of food/fasting and episodes, access to medicines or supplements, and how glucose and symptoms relate. Explain the need for prompt clinical assessment without inventing a confirmed endocrine diagnosis. Distinguish the alert review state from a recurrent severe episode: advice for unconsciousness or inability to swallow must not recommend oral food/drink; describe emergency help in the requested UK context. Do not require a rare tumour diagnosis, imaging, pathology, surgery or exact reproduction of the original article’s explanation. Exactly two purposeful questions are requested by the task. Credit defensible wording and alternatives.

cases.title: N03 — Altered consciousness and an abnormal magnesium result
cases.facts:
A 54-year-old man is brought to the emergency department within 30 minutes of being found unresponsive at a health spa. His recorded history includes treated hepatitis C and a remote appendectomy; there is no known chronic kidney disease or regular medicine use.

On arrival: blood pressure 104/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 12/min, temperature 34.3°C and Glasgow Coma Scale E3 V2 M5 (total 10). He has flaccid weakness and generalised areflexia.

Initial results: magnesium 15.8 mg/dL (laboratory reference 1.7–2.4), creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 14 mg/dL, potassium 4.8 mmol/L, arterial pH 7.183, PaCO2 50.1 mmHg and bicarbonate 18.4 mEq/L. ECG shows sinus rhythm, prominent T waves and diffuse ST depression. Non-contrast brain CT is unremarkable; screening for common drugs of abuse is negative.

The decision point is when these initial laboratory results become available after arrival, before treatment. A detailed exposure history, product information and subsequent clinical course are not supplied.

cases.title: N04 — Recurrent headache and inflammatory CSF
cases.facts:
A 36-year-old woman initially presented with five days of low-grade fever and severe headache. Her past medical history was unremarkable. Examination recorded marked meningeal signs; head CT showed no abnormality. Initial cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) contained 183 cells/µL, 97.8% lymphocytes, and protein 83.3 mg/dL. CSF PCR did not identify an infectious cause, and Borrelia serology was negative. No CSF culture result is supplied.

During that admission she received intravenous dexamethasone for nine days. Repeat CSF contained 130 cells/µL and protein 46.1 mg/dL. She improved and was discharged after 12 days on 11 March 2026.

Persistent headache and photophobia led to further emergency visits. On 14 March she was readmitted with severe orthostatic headache, upper-limb tremor and dizziness. Examination recorded neck stiffness and a positive Kernig sign. Brain MRI was normal. Spinal MRI showed L3–L4 and L4–L5 disc herniation with possible nerve-root compression. Repeat CSF contained 178 cells/µL, 97.7% lymphocytes, and protein 36.6 mg/dL.

Autoimmune antibody results and the later clinical course are not supplied at this stage. The publication does not provide an exact antibody-result reporting time; this exercise releases that information separately, not at an invented clinical timestamp.

cases.title: N05 — Gastrointestinal symptoms and cardiac abnormalities
cases.facts:
A 52-year-old man has had watery diarrhoea three to four times daily for a year, with upper-abdominal discomfort and distal numbness. Previous gastrointestinal assessment identified bile reflux gastritis and a colonic lesion that was removed; histology showed a sessile serrated lesion with dysplasia. Diarrhoea persisted. Over the preceding six months he developed exertional breathlessness, fatigue and a 10 kg weight loss.

At the initial examination, blood pressure was 80/46 mmHg and heart rate 52 beats/min. Initial NT-proBNP was 887 pg/mL, high-sensitivity troponin T 23.9 ng/L, creatinine 1.3 mg/dL and eGFR 62.7 mL/min/1.73 m². No updated vital signs are supplied for the later investigation-review point.

Echocardiography showed symmetric left-ventricular wall thickening, septal thickness 14.1 mm, LVEF 36%, grade-II diastolic dysfunction and relative apical sparing on strain. Cardiac MRI showed diffuse wall thickening, high native myocardial T1, extracellular volume 49.85%–52.47%, and diffuse subendocardial late gadolinium enhancement involving the left ventricle and interatrial septum.

Serum/urine immunofixation and serum free-light-chain testing found no monoclonal gammopathy. Alpha-galactosidase A activity was 1.70 µmol/L/h (laboratory reference >2.0); GLA sequencing found no pathogenic variant. Plasma lyso-Gb3 was not measured. Technetium-PYP scintigraphy showed planar grade-1 myocardial uptake and a heart-to-contralateral-lung ratio >1.42; acquisition timing and additional technical details are not supplied here.

This exercise stops before the subsequent biopsy/subtyping investigations. No tissue diagnosis, further genetic result, later treatment or outcome is supplied.

cases.title: N06 — Treatment timeline during circulatory support
cases.facts:
A 28-year-old man presented with circulatory shock. At 08:21 on Day 0, BP was 70/45 mmHg and heart rate 142 beats/min. Right-heart abnormalities and a femoral venous thrombus were identified. VA-ECMO started at 10:20. CT pulmonary angiography at 11:58 showed main/branch pulmonary arterial filling defects. These are extracts for a retrospective ICU record review, not a live treatment instruction.

Day-0 record:
Time | Record
11:55 | Sample: platelets 21 × 10⁹/L, haemoglobin 150 g/L, fibrinogen 1.18 g/L and aPTT 43.5 s. Result-reporting times are not supplied for this sample.
14:50–15:10 | Two institutional therapeutic doses of apheresis platelets were transfused. Other haemostatic support was recorded over 13:15–17:00.
17:00 | Unfractionated heparin (UFH) was paused and the first alteplase infusion started. No post-transfusion platelet count immediately before this infusion is supplied.
17:20 | Arterial cannulation-site bleeding was treated with compression.
17:39 | Sample: platelets 62 × 10⁹/L, haemoglobin 136 g/L, fibrinogen 1.38 g/L and aPTT 47.5 s. Result-reporting times are not supplied for this sample.
18:10 | Vasoactive infusion rates were reduced, but ECMO and vasoactive support were still needed.
19:03 | A progress note records cessation of cannulation-site bleeding after compression; a second alteplase dose was ordered.
19:25 | The second infusion started. Each infusion stage lasted approximately one hour; exact completion timestamps are unavailable.
20:13 | A coagulation sample was obtained: fibrinogen 1.07 g/L and aPTT 58.9 s.
21:06 | The coagulation results from the 20:13 sample were reported.

The treating team later reported that UFH restarted after the second infusion, approximately one hour after its 19:25 start. No independent exact restart timestamp is available. A patient-specific anticoagulation target and the documented evidence used at restart are not supplied. The subsequent clinical course and later safety adjudication are not supplied.

cases.title: CAND02 — Changing thyroid tests during pembrolizumab treatment
cases.facts:
Role/channel: record system; clinician-facing synthesis
Decision point: Researcher-defined review of records through 27 January 2023, before the March 2023 endocrine assessment and later treatment changes.
Opening: Records for a man treated for oesophageal cancer show a marked earlier TSH rise during thyroid replacement, followed by a suppressed TSH. Review the changing thyroid profile through 27 January 2023.

Prepared written snapshot: all stored facts through the selected decision point.
[record; presentation] In 2019, TT4 was 51 nmol/L with TSH 0.938 mIU/L; thyroid antibodies were elevated and ultrasound suggested Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. No intervention was undertaken. On 11 April 2022, before treatment and without replacement, TT3 was 0.93 nmol/L, TT4 53.87 nmol/L and TSH 0.82 mIU/L.

[record; presentation] Pembrolizumab 200 mg with nab-paclitaxel 400 mg and carboplatin 400 mg every 21 days began on 15 April 2022. Radical oesophagectomy was performed on 7 July 2022, followed by adjuvant pembrolizumab, paclitaxel and carboplatin. The last chemotherapy cycle was completed on 23 September 2022; pembrolizumab continued.

[record; presentation] On 6 May 2022, TT4 was 164.49 nmol/L and TSH <0.004 mIU/L. On 27 May, TT4 was 14.31 nmol/L and TSH 6.032 mIU/L; levothyroxine was started at 50 micrograms once daily.

[record; presentation] The narrative reports good levothyroxine adherence, taken fasting and separately from other medicines. Table 1 identifies the dose at sampling: 100 micrograms daily on 22 August, 22 September and 27 October 2022, then 125 micrograms daily on 21 November 2022 and 27 January 2023.

[record; presentation] On 22 August 2022, TT4 was <3.9 nmol/L and TSH 119.96 mIU/L. On 22 September, TT4 was 31.2 nmol/L and TSH 71.86 mIU/L. Both samples were recorded during 100-microgram daily levothyroxine treatment.

[record; presentation] On 27 October 2022, TT4 was 68.0 nmol/L and TSH 2.36 mIU/L during 100-microgram daily replacement. Table 1 reference intervals are TT4 55.34–160.88 nmol/L and TSH 0.35–4.94 mIU/L.

[record; presentation] On 21 November 2022, TT4 was 64.1 nmol/L and TSH 0.06 mIU/L. On 27 January 2023, TT4 was 45.8 nmol/L and TSH 0.08 mIU/L. Both samples were recorded during 125-microgram daily replacement. TT4 was within the reported interval in November and below it in January, while TSH was suppressed at both points.

cases.title: CAND03 — New symptoms during long-stable osilodrostat treatment
cases.facts:
Role/channel: record system; clinician-facing synthesis
Decision point: Early hospital assessment of the symptomatic episode after documented telephone advice and a 20-mg oral hydrocortisone dose, before release of the episode’s endocrine test packet or subsequent response.
Opening: A woman receiving long-term treatment for Cushing’s disease has new nausea, abdominal pain, muscle pain, fatigue and low home blood pressure. Symptoms persisted after telephone advice, and she is now being assessed in hospital.

Prepared written snapshot: all stored facts through the selected decision point.
[record; presentation] The patient was 52 at the earlier diagnostic presentation, when ACTH-dependent Cushing’s syndrome and a pituitary origin were supported. Transsphenoidal surgery did not achieve biochemical remission; hypertension persisted and she declined immediate reoperation. The earlier work-up also diagnosed diabetes and insulin resistance. This age is not assigned to the current episode.

[record; presentation] Ketoconazole was ultimately stopped because hepatotoxicity recurred. Metyrapone was later used for 36 weeks and stopped because its study ended, despite biochemical control and good adherence. Osilodrostat was then begun at 2 mg twice daily.

[record; presentation] The symptoms began two years after osilodrostat initiation while she was receiving a stable total dose of 4 mg daily, without recent dose escalation. Earlier treatment had produced substantial biochemical and clinical improvement.

[record; presentation] At symptom onset she reported nausea, abdominal pain, myalgia and fatigue. Home blood pressure was 98/67 mmHg, with heart rate over 100 beats per minute. No hospital vital-sign values are supplied in this source packet.

[record; presentation] She was advised to stop osilodrostat, take hydrocortisone 20 mg orally and attend the next morning. She took the advised actions, but symptoms persisted and hospital assessment followed. The source does not specify the interval between hydrocortisone and the subsequent cortisol sample.

[record; presentation] Dosing errors were excluded in the report; documented treatment adherence since the previous visit was 98%.

[record; presentation] The episode’s Table 1B reports 08:00 cortisol 0.38 micrograms/dL (reference 4.82–19.5), ACTH 66.3 pg/mL (6.0–56.0) and DHEA-S 0.09 micromol/L (0.51–5.56). The narrative places confirmation during hospitalisation, without giving sample timing relative to the prior hydrocortisone dose.

cases.title: CAND04 — Severe kidney injury after a febrile gastrointestinal illness
cases.facts:
Role/channel: record system; clinician-facing synthesis
Decision point: Initial admission work-up, before next-day NGS evidence, definitive renal pathology and treatment response. Initial laboratory and non-contrast imaging records are requestable.
Opening: A 74-year-old woman is admitted with worsening dyspnoea, leg oedema and markedly reduced urine output after a febrile illness with gastrointestinal symptoms. Assess current danger and the main explanations for the renal presentation.

Prepared written snapshot: all stored facts through the selected decision point.
[record; presentation] Two weeks before admission she developed fever after a long-haul flight, peaking at 38.8°C, with nausea, diarrhoea and poor appetite. Fever and diarrhoea improved after acetaminophen and rifaximin. One week before admission she developed oliguria, reported as 350 mL/day, and dyspnoea, which progressed.

[record; presentation] Admission findings were heart rate 106/min, temperature 36.5°C, blood pressure 130/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 28/min and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. There were bilateral pulmonary crackles, moderate lower-limb pitting oedema and dullness on bladder percussion. Abdominal, rebound and renal tenderness were absent.

[record; presentation] She had hypertension and hyperlipidaemia for 10 years and type 2 diabetes for 20 years. Recorded medicines were felodipine, atorvastatin, aspirin, metformin and insulin. Acetaminophen and rifaximin were used during the preceding illness.

[record; presentation] The initial laboratory table reports creatinine 689 micromol/L, urea nitrogen 66.3 mmol/L, potassium 7.11 mmol/L, phosphate 3.98 mmol/L, calcium 1.86 mmol/L and carbon dioxide combining power 5.5 mmol/L. The documented creatinine baseline was 65 micromol/L six months before admission. No measured blood-gas pH is supplied.

[record; presentation] The table reports WBC 52.85 ×10^9/L, neutrophils 97.8%, CRP 96 mg/L and procalcitonin 5.9 ng/mL. Urine had marked pyuria and haematuria; flow-cytometry WBC was 41,905/microlitre, RBC 15,125/microlitre and bacteria 7,698/microlitre. UPCR was 1,655 mg/g creatinine and UACR 415.3 mg/g creatinine; reported 24-hour total protein was 598 mg.

[record; presentation] Non-contrast CT showed bilateral renal enlargement and cortical thickening, with an ill-defined relatively hypoattenuating area at the left upper pole. Ultrasound showed bilateral enlargement and cortical swelling without hydronephrosis or abscess. Contrast CT was not performed because of AKI; acute-phase MRI was not performed because her clinical condition precluded safe transport/examination. These are missing investigations, not negative contrast/MRI findings.

[record; presentation] The report states that a single 0.5-g IV meropenem dose was given on the day of admission before conventional blood and urine cultures were collected. NGS blood and urine samples were collected the day after admission. Microbiological results are outside this initial review packet; no culture-based susceptibility result is available in the report.

cases.title: CAND07 — Syncope, oedema and marked proteinuria in a patient with lymphoma
cases.facts:
Role/channel: record system; clinician-facing synthesis
Decision point: First-admission diagnostic review after the reported initial studies and adrenal-insufficiency treatment, before the scheduled outpatient renal biopsy and four-week follow-up. Exact within-admission result times are unspecified.
Opening: An 80-year-old woman with lymphoma and cardiac comorbidity is admitted after witnessed syncope. She is hypotensive, has substantial leg oedema and has newly recognised proteinuria. Assess the immediate problem and the renal/systemic differential.

Prepared written snapshot: all stored facts through the selected decision point.
[record; presentation] The episode was preceded by progressive lightheadedness and tunnel vision, followed by brief loss of consciousness and rapid spontaneous recovery. Admission blood pressure was 86/58 mmHg. Examination showed significant bilateral lower-limb pitting oedema and generalised fatigue. No later/current repeat vital-sign values are supplied.

[record; presentation] She had non-Hodgkin lymphoma previously treated with a rituximab-based regimen, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, hypertension and coronary artery disease. The initial history does not establish a definitive lymphoma subclassification.

[record; presentation] Initial neurological and cardiac evaluations, including investigation for arrhythmia and structural disease, were reported as unrevealing. Admission echocardiography showed EF 60–65%, normal left-ventricular thickness and trivial regurgitation. These findings are not a tissue evaluation for systemic deposition disease.

[record; presentation] The admission column of Table 1 reports urine protein 3+, creatinine 1.8 mg/dL, BUN 45.0 mg/dL, albumin 3.0 g/dL and UPCR 10 g/g. No measured pre-illness creatinine is supplied.

[record; presentation] Admission serum lambda free light chain was 131 mg/L, kappa 14.41 mg/L and kappa/lambda ratio 0.11. Serum immunofixation showed an IgM monoclonal lambda gammopathy.

[record; presentation] Admission C3 was 78 mg/dL and C4 9.7 mg/dL; source reference intervals were not supplied. Hepatitis C antibody was positive, but HCV RNA and cryoglobulins were not detected. P-ANCA/C-ANCA were negative.

[record; presentation] During the first admission she was also diagnosed with adrenal insufficiency and treated with hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone. The report supplies no confirmatory cortisol/ACTH results, doses or exact timing within the admission, and does not establish that this explained all findings.

[record; presentation] The admission assessment was nephrotic syndrome of uncertain cause, and an outpatient renal biopsy was scheduled. Renal tissue and later marrow findings are not supplied at this decision point.

cases.title: CAND08 — Seizure, behavioural change and kidney allograft dysfunction
cases.facts:
Role/channel: caregiver and record system
Decision point: Transfer admission, designated Day 0 in the report. Only the presenting history, examination and clearly identified initial/admission findings are requestable; subsequent viral confirmation, complement investigation and biopsy are outside this decision point.
Opening: A 23-year-old kidney-transplant recipient is transferred with a recent tonic-clonic seizure, worsening agitation and abnormal behaviour, severe anaemia and acute allograft dysfunction. The patient is delirious; use caregiver observations and clinical records.

Prepared written snapshot: all stored facts through the selected decision point.
[record; presentation] She received a deceased-donor kidney transplant six years earlier for end-stage renal disease. The reported maintenance regimen before presentation was tacrolimus 1.5 mg twice daily, mycophenolate mofetil 360 mg twice daily and prednisone 8 mg daily.

[caregiver; presentation] About two weeks before this admission she developed throat discomfort and a productive cough. The symptoms did not improve with levofloxacin.

[caregiver; presentation] A tonic-clonic seizure occurred about one week before admission, followed by progressively agitated and abnormal behaviour. Neurological symptoms worsened despite symptomatic treatment at the local hospital, leading to transfer.

[record; presentation] On Day 0 she was delirious and appeared pale. Temperature was 36.8 °C, pulse 91/min, respiratory rate 19/min and blood pressure 141/85 mmHg.

[record; presentation] The initial work-up described anaemia, thrombocytopenia and schistocytes. Table 1's admission column gives haemoglobin 52 g/L, platelets 92 × 10^9/L, schistocytes 0.8%, haptoglobin 0.126 g/L and LDH 262 U/L.

[record; presentation] The local work-up had identified acute allograft dysfunction. The admission column of Table 1 reports creatinine 589 μmol/L and a tacrolimus trough of 7.30 ng/mL. A measured pre-illness creatinine is not given in this packet.

[record; presentation] Profound CD4 T-cell lymphopenia was described in the initial work-up. Table 1's admission values include CD3 58 cells/μL, CD4 20 cells/μL, CD8 37 cells/μL and CD4/CD8 ratio 0.53.

[record; presentation] The initial lumbar-puncture account describes raised intracranial pressure without pleocytosis. The table records an opening pressure above 320 mmH2O. CSF protein is not reproduced because the narrative and table do not agree on the biochemical description.

cases.title: CAND09 — Subacute ocular movements and gait instability with unrevealing initial tests
cases.facts:
Role/channel: patient and record system
Decision point: Reconstructed initial-admission review, before immunotherapy or follow-up. History, examination, initial MRI/CSF and standard antibody-panel findings are requestable. The tissue-based assay is deliberately withheld experimentally; the article includes it in the initial diagnostic work-up and does not establish a separate later date.
Opening: A 60-year-old man has one month of progressively blurred vision, dizziness and gait instability with frequent abnormal eye movements.

Prepared written snapshot: all stored facts through the selected decision point.
[patient; presentation] Blurred vision, dizziness and walking difficulty have progressed over about a month. I have not had double vision, limb weakness or a febrile illness since this began.

[patient; presentation] The reported earlier medical history is unremarkable. There is no reported smoking, alcohol abuse or neurotoxin exposure, and no reported family history of autoimmune, neurological or neoplastic disease.

[record; presentation] Admission vital signs and systemic examination were normal. There was continuous ocular flutter, a mild horizontal head/neck tremor, a broad-based gait and unsteadiness with eyes open or closed. Pupils and eye-movement range were normal; limb strength and pinprick/vibration sensation were preserved, reflexes were symmetric and Babinski signs absent.

[record; presentation] Initial CSF opening pressure was normal, with white cells 12 × 10^6/L and normal protein, glucose and chloride. CSF pathogen mNGS was negative. Oligoclonal bands and the IgG index were not assessed.

[record; presentation] High-resolution brain MRI with and without contrast showed no acute infarct, demyelination or structural brainstem/cerebellar lesion; the figure description also reports no abnormal contrast enhancement in those regions.

[record; presentation] Routine peripheral blood tests, comprehensive metabolic panels and thyroid function were reported as unremarkable or normal. B lymphocytes were increased at 915/μL and 31.38% against the article's stated reference ranges; T-cell and NK-cell quantities were within those ranges.

[record; presentation] The reported commercial fixed cell-based and immunoblot tests for established neural antibodies were negative, including the listed neuronal, demyelinating, onconeural and ganglioside targets. This statement concerns the standard specific-antibody panels; the tissue-based assay is outside this experimental packet.

[record; presentation] At the initial presentation there were no reported weight-loss or gastrointestinal symptoms. Serum CEA, CA19-9 and AFP were within normal limits. Endoscopy and whole-body PET-CT were deferred; they were not negative investigations.

cases.title: CAND10 — Childhood neurological symptoms revisited after adult seizures and cognitive difficulty
cases.facts:
Role/channel: caregiver and record system
Decision point: A researcher-designed pre-confirmation review during the admission at age 24. The age-based history, adult examination, EEG and structural imaging are requestable; biopsy, genetics and subsequent treatment are excluded. The report does not provide exact dates or a complete sequence within that admission.
Opening: A 24-year-old woman is admitted for recurrent episodes of impaired consciousness preceded by headache and blurred vision. She has substantial cognitive difficulty, so obtain the longitudinal history from a caregiver and objective findings from records.

Prepared written snapshot: all stored facts through the selected decision point.
[caregiver; presentation] The first recorded symptoms were brief headache and visual-disturbance episodes at about age six, lasting several minutes.

[caregiver; presentation] Learning difficulties appeared at about seven, with persistently poor primary-school performance. Between ages 15 and 21, no substantial neurological deterioration was reported.

[caregiver; presentation] At age 22 she had a probable focal seizure progressing to a bilateral tonic-clonic event while cycling, preceded by headache and blurred vision, with incontinence and foaming at the mouth. From 22 to 24, episodes recurred once or twice monthly.

[caregiver; presentation] The family noticed further memory and everyday cognitive difficulty in early adulthood, especially after recurrent seizures began. This is a reported change on top of longstanding learning difficulty; the report has no serial standardized cognitive assessments to quantify that change.

[caregiver; presentation] The parents were reported to be clinically healthy and were not consanguineous. Her younger brother reported mild memory difficulty but remained functionally independent; he had not undergone the genetic testing described in the report.

[record; presentation] At admission, muscle strength, sensation and gait were normal, and the ophthalmological examination was unremarkable. MMSE was 12. Formal neuropsychological testing beyond MMSE was not completed.

[record; presentation] The admission EEG showed sharp and slow waves in the bilateral occipital and parietal regions.

[record; presentation] At age six, CT had shown small intracranial calcifications. At the adult admission, CT showed widespread basal-ganglia and cerebellar calcifications and two cystic lesions with fluid levels. MRI showed right thalamic and parietal cysts plus diffuse periventricular/deep-white-matter T2/FLAIR hyperintensity, without diffusion restriction or contrast enhancement.

cases.title: CAND11 — Acute neurological deterioration following complicated retinal surgery
cases.facts:
Role/channel: record system only; emergency-team review
Decision point: Approximately one hour after the April 8, 2025 retinal operation, at the onset of acute neurological deterioration and before imaging results are supplied. This is a record-based emergency assessment, not a patient interview.
Opening: A 61-year-old woman develops sudden altered mental status, slurred speech and gait instability about one hour after retinal surgery, rapidly losing the ability to walk independently. Review the perioperative records for the emergency team.

Prepared written snapshot: all stored facts through the selected decision point.
[record; presentation] The recorded history included right cataract surgery in 2020 with good recovery. The report records no hypertension, diabetes, stroke, arrhythmia, thrombotic disease, smoking, alcohol use or hereditary disorder.

[record; presentation] She was admitted on April 7, 2025 after seven days of right-eye visual loss and shadowing. Examination and ocular imaging showed a macula-involving rhegmatogenous retinal detachment; vitrectomy with laser and perfluorocarbon liquid was planned.

[record; presentation] On April 8, standard three-port pars plana vitrectomy was performed under local anaesthesia with subretinal-fluid drainage. The retina reattached after heavy-liquid injection. Deterioration occurred while the team was preparing for silicone-oil tamponade.

[record; presentation] She suddenly reported severe ocular pain, sweating and a near-death sensation during the operation. Pulse oximetry transiently fell to 88%. No post-deterioration full set of vital signs is supplied in this packet.

[record; presentation] The surgeon observed a dome-shaped choroidal elevation and suspected expulsive suprachoroidal haemorrhage. Estimated blood loss was 2 mL, confined to the posterior segment without anterior-chamber involvement or globe rupture. The record does not document direct observation of air entering the circulation.

[record; presentation] The procedure was immediately stopped, with 3 mL of perfluorocarbon liquid retained. The sclerotomies were closed, and intravenous hemocoagulase and tranexamic acid were given. Their doses are not supplied.

[record; presentation] About one hour postoperatively she developed abrupt altered mental status, slurred speech and gait instability, quickly progressing to inability to ambulate independently. The packet stops at this emergency review, before the subsequent imaging and laboratory results.

cases.title: CAND12 — Recurrent late-onset seizures with worsening memory and age-75 investigation findings
cases.facts:
Role/channel: record system; longitudinal clinician review
Decision point: Reconstructed review of the first comprehensive admission at age 75 (Ex. 1), restricted to clinical observations and sample findings assigned to age 75 or earlier. The published age-75 amyloid concentrations are supplied as retrospective research records, not asserted to have been available to the treating team during that admission.
Opening: A 75-year-old man with late-onset focal seizures is admitted for worsening memory and seizures that have become daily. Review the available longitudinal records and the first comprehensive investigation packet.

Prepared written snapshot: all stored facts through the selected decision point.
[record; presentation] At age 60, a right-handed man with 16 years of education presented with transient forgetfulness. At 61, episodes involved olfactory hallucinations followed by blank staring and oral automatisms. Routine EEG initially showed no apparent epileptiform activity, but the clinical diagnosis was medial temporal lobe epilepsy.

[record; presentation] Carbamazepine was stopped after a drug eruption. Valproate monotherapy, reported at up to 800 mg/day, was associated with seizure remission by age 64. Gabapentin was added at age 74 after recurrent seizures and right frontotemporal sharp waves on repeated EEG; its dose and the exact current valproate dose are not supplied here.

[record; presentation] At age 70 he noticed mild memory difficulty: MMSE was 29 and WMS-R Logical Memory II delayed recall was 11/50. Forgetfulness worsened, and delayed recall was 6 at age 74. The narrative reports further worsening by admission at 75 but does not supply an exact age-75 cognitive score in this packet.

[record; presentation] Focal impaired-awareness seizures recurred at age 72 after earlier remission, increased by 74 and became daily by the admission at 75 despite treatment.

[record; presentation] At 74, brain MRI including susceptibility-weighted sequences showed mild diffuse atrophy without hippocampal sclerosis, microbleeds, amyloid-angiopathy features or significant vascular burden. FDG-PET showed no significant hypometabolism. At 75, repeat MRI and FDG-PET showed no significant interval change. No age-75 amyloid PET result is supplied.

[record; presentation] At 75, 24-hour video EEG recorded six clinical seizures with ictal discharges arising in the left frontotemporal region and spreading through the left hemisphere. Table 1 also lists interictal spike/sharp-wave and sharp-transient counts, but explicitly states that sharp transients were not definitively epileptiform.

[record; presentation] For the age-75 Ex. 1 sample, the published CSF results are Aβ40 13,671 pg/mL; Aβ42 1,549 pg/mL (reported reference >674); Aβ42/40 ratio 0.113 (reported reference >0.118); and p-tau 74.6 pg/mL (reported reference <50.0). These are the retrospective published sample results; real-time availability of the amyloid values at 75 is not asserted.

[record; presentation] The first lumbar puncture was at 75, so pre-epilepsy CSF biomarker levels are unknown. The article states that stored Aβ samples were measured in duplicate in one analytical batch after one freeze-thaw cycle; p-tau was measured during routine practice at each puncture. Timing of cognitive testing relative to recent seizures was not systematically recorded.

cases.title: CAND13 — Recurrent gastrointestinal bleeding four months after liver transplantation
cases.facts:
Role/channel: emergency clinician record review
Decision point: First bleeding episode four months after transplantation, after initial and repeat endoscopy but before the first angiogram or embolization. All available replies are records; the patient is not required to narrate an urgent bleeding episode.
Opening: A liver-transplant recipient has recurrent vomiting of blood, dark-red rectal bleeding and right upper abdominal pain four months after transplantation. Bleeding and progressive anaemia have persisted.

Prepared written snapshot: all stored facts through the selected decision point.
[record; presentation] The patient is a 23-year-old man. Repeated bright-red haematemesis, about 50 mL per episode, was followed by dark-red haematochezia. Dull right upper quadrant pain, regurgitation, fatigue, dizziness, blurred vision and sweating accompanied the bleeding.

[record; presentation] Orthotopic deceased-donor liver transplantation was performed in 2024 for end-stage alcohol-related cirrhosis. Before transplantation he had repeated decompensation and plasma exchange; oesophagogastric variceal bleeding was treated endoscopically in 2023.

[record; presentation] The donor right hepatic artery arose from the superior mesenteric artery. Reconstruction joined donor common hepatic artery to recipient right hepatic artery and donor right hepatic artery to recipient gastroduodenal artery. The portal vein and common bile duct had end-to-end reconstruction.

[record; presentation] Initial post-transplant immunosuppression comprised tacrolimus, enteric-coated mycophenolate sodium and corticosteroids, later adjusted. No antiplatelet or systemic anticoagulant treatment was documented in the immediate postoperative period; this does not establish the current medication list.

[record; presentation] On postoperative days 6–8 he had fever and Enterococcus faecium bacteraemia, with positive SARS-CoV-2 testing. Fever resolved by day 9 after treatment. Imaging showed fluid collections without definite bile leakage or a localised infectious focus; bile culture was negative.

[record; presentation] Earlier surveillance Doppler examinations showed patent hepatic arterial flow, with transient resistance or flow abnormalities that improved. No focal arterial lesion or pseudoaneurysm had been identified during that earlier surveillance.

[record; presentation] Initial upper endoscopy found a duodenal bulb ulcer without observed active bleeding; no endoscopic haemostasis was performed. Continued bleeding prompted repeat endoscopy: removing a clot at the major duodenal papilla revealed fresh blood oozing from the papillary orifice.

[record; presentation] Progressive anaemia during persistent bleeding is documented. A numerical blood pressure, pulse, coagulation panel and time-stamped haemoglobin specifically before the first angiogram are not supplied in this packet. Current severity measurements must be obtained rather than assumed normal.

This is recurrent overt gastrointestinal bleeding with progressive anaemia in a recent liver-transplant recipient. Dizziness, sweating and ongoing blood loss require immediate senior assessment, haemodynamic monitoring and preparation for haemorrhage management; the absence of supplied vital signs must not imply stability. Obtain current blood count, coagulation studies, crossmatch and relevant renal and graft tests while engaging gastroenterology and the transplant team.

The initial differential includes recurrent portal-hypertensive bleeding, peptic ulcer bleeding and a hepatobiliary or transplant vascular source. Prior varices create a plausible competing explanation, but neither history nor an ulcer alone localises the current bleeding. If the repeat endoscopic record is received, fresh blood from the major papilla strongly supports haemobilia and should prompt urgent vascular localisation with interventional radiology and transplant surgery. The exact lesion and arterial-biliary communication remain unconfirmed before angiography.

Review the reconstruction, immunosuppression and postoperative infectious history. Earlier patent Doppler flow does not exclude a subsequently developing vascular lesion. Past bacteraemia raises a question about infection without proving an infected pseudoaneurysm. Further diagnostic and haemostatic decisions must account for graft arterial perfusion. Do not use later embolization, surgical findings, pathology, deterioration or death to justify the initial conclusion. The later death mechanism was never definitively established; it is not a required diagnostic target.

cases.title: CAND14 — Jaundice, abdominal pain and fever after prior hepatectomy
cases.facts:
Role/channel: patient and record system
Decision point: Admission assessment five months after outside hepatectomy, before ERCP, removed-material pathology and treatment response. The pre-ERCP MRCP/CT packet is requestable experimentally; its release is not a claim that imaging was completed at the instant of admission.
Opening: A 70-year-old woman develops progressive jaundice over two weeks with intermittent abdominal pain, then three days of fever reaching 40.0 °C. She underwent liver surgery five months earlier.

Prepared written snapshot: all stored facts through the selected decision point.
[patient; presentation] Yellowing of my skin and eyes increased over two weeks, with intermittent abdominal pain. Fever began three days before admission and reached 40.0 °C.

[record; presentation] She had hepatitis C for 15 years. Left hepatectomy and cholecystectomy for a cirrhotic nodule were performed elsewhere five months before admission. Available records report no postoperative complications.

[record; presentation] The original hepatectomy operative report is unavailable. The outside pathology report describes chronic hepatitis and nodular cirrhosis, with no definite neoplastic change. The available material cannot identify a specific operative vascular, thermal or biliary injury.

[record; presentation] Admission total bilirubin was 234.0 μmol/L and direct bilirubin 182.4; ALP 155 U/L, GGT 172, AST 88 and ALT 64. Albumin was 38 g/L and INR 1.11.

[record; presentation] Admission CRP was 188.60 mg/L, procalcitonin 9.49 ng/mL, white cells 4.10 × 10^9/L with 93.8% neutrophils, and platelets 76 × 10^9/L. Creatinine was 73 μmol/L and lactate 0.8 mmol/L. No further high fever was recorded after admission. Blood and bile cultures were not performed.

[record; presentation] Available pre-ERCP MRCP shows intrahepatic and extrahepatic duct dilatation with sludge-like common-bile-duct material. The common bile duct measures about 19 mm and the largest intrahepatic duct about 9 mm. CT shows heterogeneous intraductal material.

[record; presentation] The pre-ERCP contrast CT describes a patent hepatic artery supplying the remaining liver, without visible stenosis, occlusion or thrombosis. This is a large-vessel observation, not proof against every prior or localised ischaemic injury.

Jaundice, abdominal pain and recent high fever after hepatectomy require urgent assessment for biliary obstruction with possible acute cholangitis. Assess haemodynamics, mental state and organ function, obtain appropriate cultures if feasible, and involve the hepatobiliary or endoscopy service promptly. The absence of further high fever after admission does not erase the preceding illness. Treatment and drainage decisions should follow the current severity and local specialist pathway.

If the admission laboratory packet is received, marked predominantly direct hyperbilirubinaemia and raised inflammatory markers strengthen this concern. A near-normal total white-cell count does not negate the high neutrophil fraction or other inflammatory evidence. If imaging is received, substantial duct dilatation with heterogeneous common-duct material supports mechanical obstruction. Stones or sludge, postoperative narrowing, clot or tissue debris and tumour-related obstruction remain considerations; imaging alone cannot establish the material’s histology.

Review the outside operation and pathology. The operative report is explicitly unavailable, so a request for it is still appropriate and should be credited. Chronic hepatitis with cirrhosis and no definite neoplasia were reported in the outside specimen. A patent visible hepatic artery does not establish that all earlier microvascular injury is absent. The five-month sequence supports temporal association only; no specific surgical injury, necrotic epithelial pathology, cast morphology or later improvement should be asserted from the initial evidence.

cases.title: CAND15 — A child with epigastric fullness, pallor and a palpable mass

Role/channel: caregiver and record system
Decision point: Initial paediatric assessment, before upper endoscopy or a removal decision. Diagnostic blood tests and the pre-endoscopy CT are separate requestable experimental packets; their release does not imply actual tests were completed at first contact.

Prepared written snapshot: all stored facts through the selected decision point.
[caregiver; presentation] She has had dull upper abdominal pain and fullness after meals for a week. Her appetite is poor. She has not had nausea or vomiting, and her bowel habits have remained normal.

[caregiver; presentation] We first noticed her eating hair when she was two. We interrupted the behaviour when we saw it and believed she had stopped completely in recent years. That is our belief, rather than a medically confirmed absence of the behaviour.

[caregiver; presentation] She has not had formal psychiatric intervention or follow-up to establish whether the hair-eating behaviour actually stopped.

[record; presentation] Examination documents fatigue, pale lips and conjunctivae, asymmetric abdominal distension and a firm, non-tender, clearly demarcated epigastric mass about 12 × 6 cm, with limited mobility. No peritoneal irritation was noted.

[record; presentation] Haemoglobin was 77 g/L, haematocrit 0.267 L/L, serum iron 3.1 μmol/L and ferritin 6.3 ng/mL. Faecal occult blood was weakly positive.

[record; presentation] Total protein was 53.2 g/L, albumin 33.5 g/L and prealbumin 88.6 mg/L; the report describes hypoproteinaemia.

[record; presentation] Available contrast abdominal CT shows a heterogeneous intragastric mass about 6 × 12 cm, considered suspicious for a foreign body or trichobezoar. No extension beyond the stomach was identified on this study. Endoscopic confirmation is outside this packet.

cases.facts:
Role/channel: emergency clinician record review
Decision point: Emergency admission on 8 October 2024, before treatment response, discharge or decisions about resuming immunotherapy. All channels are records because drowsiness is part of the acute presentation. Reported admission results are requestable; no turnaround times are inferred.
Opening: An adult man treated for renal cancer presents to the emergency department with three days of fatigue, drowsiness and blurred vision, followed by one day of nausea and vomiting.

Prepared written snapshot: all stored facts through the selected decision point.
[record; presentation] The emergency presentation on 8 October 2024 followed three days of fatigue, drowsiness and blurred vision and one day of nausea and vomiting.

[record; presentation] Right radical nephrectomy in January 2019 confirmed clear-cell renal carcinoma. Pembrolizumab 200 mg IV every three weeks plus axitinib 5 mg twice daily began in April 2023 for suspected pulmonary metastases. He had completed 22 immunotherapy cycles by the acute presentation.

Examination recorded clear consciousness despite the preceding drowsiness, poor general condition and an acute appearance. Weight was 65 kg, height 180 cm and BMI 20.1 kg/m². No obvious cardiopulmonary or abdominal abnormality was found.

[record; presentation] Admission glucose was 37.9 mmol/L, urine ketones 3+, pH 7.15, bicarbonate 9.8 mmol/L, base excess −17.6 mmol/L and lactate 4.6 mmol/L. Sodium was 128 mmol/L.

[record; presentation] Admission HbA1c was 6.7% and fasting C-peptide was below 0.3 ng/mL. GAD, islet-cell and insulin autoantibodies were negative. These are reported admission findings, released on request experimentally without implying that all were available immediately.

[record; presentation] The saved case paragraph does not supply admission potassium, renal function or a measured blood ketone concentration; it refers to supplementary laboratory tables. Those values are not supplied or assumed normal in this case packet.

cases.title: CAND21 — Progressive breathlessness despite repeated treatment for a COPD exacerbation
cases.facts:
Role/channel: patient and record system in the early communicative phase
Decision point: Early admission, while requiring 2 L/min nasal-cannula oxygen and before day-3 BAL or later antibody results, ventilation, transfer and ECMO. Opening: A 65-year-old woman with COPD has one month of worsening breathlessness after cough and wheeze. She has not improved with outpatient treatment and now needs supplemental oxygen at admission.

Prepared written snapshot: all stored facts through the selected decision point.
[patient; presentation] My breathing has worsened over about a month. It began with cough and wheeze; later I developed fever, chills and general weakness.

[patient; presentation] I smoke tobacco daily. I recently resumed vaping after having stopped seven years earlier.

[patient; presentation] No relevant occupational or environmental exposure, medication-related pulmonary risk factor, diabetes or other known cause of immunocompromise was reported. Details beyond those documented categories are not supplied.

[record; presentation] The recorded background includes COPD and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease.

[patient; presentation] For presumed COPD exacerbation I received two courses of steroids; the second was combined with ten days of doxycycline. I did not improve clinically.

[record; presentation] At admission she had hypoxaemic respiratory failure requiring 2 L/min oxygen by nasal cannula. Infection, inhalational injury, inflammatory or interstitial disease and other diffuse alveolar processes remain possibilities, alongside relevant cardiopulmonary alternatives. Negative viral tests or procalcitonin alone do not eliminate every infection.

Vaping exposure supplies a plausible clue but does not prove causation. The early CT pattern is not diagnostic of a specific proteinosis or injury mechanism. cases.facts:
A woman in her early 70s with metastatic non-small-cell lung cancer developed generalised oedema during treatment.
Amivantamab started four months earlier. Oedema began after the first dose and extended to the abdominal wall over two weeks. Previous treatment included osimertinib and carboplatin/pemetrexed. She has hypertension treated with an ACE inhibitor.
Albumin fell from 4.6 to 2.1 g/dL. Creatinine is 1.83 mg/dL, previously 1.1. Blood pressure is 130/70 mm Hg, pulse 86/min, respiratory rate 18/min, temperature 36.8°C and oxygen saturation 97%. Lungs are clear and no jugular venous distension is reported.
Urine protein:creatinine ratio is 246 mg/g, with negligible microalbuminuria. Liver tests and echocardiographic function are normal. Faecal alpha-1-antitrypsin is negative and recent cancer imaging is stable. No subsequent drug-withdrawal response is supplied.

cases.title: B02 — Severe low glucose after kidney–pancreas transplantation
cases.facts:
A man in his 30s with type 1 diabetes received a kidney–pancreas transplant. Early delayed renal graft function required one dialysis session and then recovered.
He takes tacrolimus, mycophenolate and tapering prednisone, with antimicrobial prophylaxis. TMP-SMX 80/400 mg daily was stopped on post-transplant day 25 because of hyperkalaemia and replaced by pentamidine.
TMP-SMX was restarted on day 69, when creatinine was stable at 0.75–0.88 mg/dL and tacrolimus trough levels were 5.5–7.5. On days 73–75 he developed weakness and dizziness with home glucose readings of 28, 33 and 36 mg/dL.
No paired venous glucose, insulin or C-peptide sample was obtained during these episodes. C-peptide values of 2–3.9 ng/mL were measured at other post-transplant times, not during the lows. The response to changing prophylaxis is not supplied.

C-peptide measured outside an episode cannot demonstrate inappropriate insulin secretion during that episode. Consider concurrent immunosuppression, renal status, intake and other causes, with transplant-team review and appropriately timed confirmatory sampling when clinically feasible; urgent care must not wait for a diagnostic sample.

cases.title: B03 — Long-lasting diarrhoea and severe weight loss
cases.facts:
A woman in her late 70s has had watery, non-bloody diarrhoea for 14 months, up to ten times daily and at night, with weight falling from 82.6 to 56.1 kg.
She has taken combination antihypertensives containing olmesartan for approximately three years. Hydrochlorothiazide was removed from the combination about 14 months ago; olmesartan continued. Duodenal biopsies showed villous blunting. Coeliac serology was negative while she was still eating gluten; later tests were also negative on a gluten-free diet.
Pancreatic enzymes for a low faecal elastase, rifaximin and dietary treatment did not resolve symptoms. Repeat elastase was normal. Symptoms improved during two admissions when her usual combination tablet was not supplied, then worsened after discharge. A short budesonide course overlapped with other treatment changes.
At this admission blood pressure is 104/62, pulse 88/min, albumin 2.3 g/dL, potassium 2.8 mmol/L, magnesium 0.7 mg/dL and phosphate 1.9 mg/dL. No response to deliberate medication withdrawal is yet known.

cases.title: B04 — Neurological symptoms around childbirth
cases.facts:
A primigravid woman in her 30s delivered at 41 weeks after induction following prolonged rupture of membranes. Her husband noticed slowed and incoherent speech before birth. She had no hypotonic intravenous fluid during labour. Oxytocin 5 IU was given only after birth.
After vacuum-assisted delivery and repair of a 3B tear, estimated blood loss was 450 mL. She was weak with blood pressure 92/45 mm Hg. Maternal sodium is 111 mmol/L and osmolality 256 mOsm/kg; a blood gas four hours earlier already showed hyponatraemia that was not acted on.
Her baby had Apgar scores of 8 at 1, 5 and 10 minutes. Three hours after birth the baby developed seizures, sodium 118 mmol/L, osmolality 243 mOsm/kg and cerebral oedema.
Further history records around 4 L of water daily and about 6 L during the preceding 24 hours. Subsequent sodium correction and clinical outcomes are not supplied.

Distinguish observed facts, hypotheses and proposed actions. Do not invent results, doses, probabilities or events. Give concise clinical justifications, not a private reasoning trace.

cases.title: B05 — Very low platelets after hip surgery
cases.facts:
A man in his 80s underwent hip-fracture surgery. He received unfractionated heparin before surgery and dalteparin afterwards. A later dalteparin dose was withheld because of haematuria after catheterisation. Levetiracetam was also newly prescribed.
On postoperative day 6 platelets were 5×10^9/L and haemoglobin 98 g/L; the blood film showed schistocytes and a leucoerythroblastic picture. Anti-PF4 ELISA was strongly positive, with optical densities 2.64 and 2.71.
The first serotonin-release assay was reported as inconclusive, not negative: strong release occurred even without heparin and the initial inhibition experiment did not resolve interpretation.
By day 9 fibrinogen was 1.8 g/L, D-dimer 63,355 ng/mL, PT 14 s and INR 1.2. Proximal deep-vein thromboses were found in both legs. Subsequent specialised assays and treatment response are not supplied.
cases.task: Audience: a clinician. Use 200–280 words in English. Synthesise the haemorrhagic and thrombotic picture, explain how the discordant test information should be interpreted, and give immediate priorities for specialist review. Do not treat an inconclusive assay as a negative result or provide an anticoagulant dose. Use only the information supplied at this decision point. Distinguish observed facts, hypotheses and proposed actions. Do not invent results, doses, probabilities or events. Give concise clinical justifications, not a private reasoning trace.
