cases.reference: The combination of heparin exposure, profound thrombocytopenia, thrombosis and strongly positive PF4 testing raises urgent concern for an immune heparin-associated process, including an atypical functional assay pattern. An inconclusive test cannot exclude it. Consider competing explanations for microangiopathy/DIC and use specialist interpretation. Urgent haematology-led decisions must balance thrombosis and bleeding; do not assert a later confirmed subtype or write a fixed treatment regimen from undisclosed evidence.

interview.decision_point: Postoperative day 9, after thrombocytopenia, thrombosis and an initially inconclusive functional assay, before specialised repeat testing.

cases.title: B06 — Worsening headache and forehead swelling in a teenager
cases.facts:
A previously well teenage boy had two weeks of upper-respiratory and sinus symptoms, followed by four days of severe retro-orbital headache. For months he had trained for 3–5 hours daily in a 12-foot pool, including breath-holding at depth without compressed air. He felt a forehead pop and pain while at depth, not during ascent.
He was initially treated for sinusitis. He returned with fever, forehead swelling and periorbital swelling, worse on the right. Temperature is 39.2°C and pulse 103/min. White cells are 7.6×10^9/L, CRP 7.3 mg/L and ESR 31 mm/hour.
CT shows a frontal sinus abscess with a subperiosteal collection, without demonstrated intracranial or orbital extension. MRI evidence of marrow involvement has not been obtained. Drainage findings, cultures and subsequent outcome are not supplied.
cases.task: Audience: a clinician. Use 200–280 words in English. Provide a clinical synthesis and immediate next steps. Explain why the new presentation changes the significance of the initial sinusitis diagnosis and what CT does and does not establish. Discuss the training history without asserting that it proved the cause. Use only the information supplied at this decision point. Distinguish observed facts, hypotheses and proposed actions. Do not invent results, doses, probabilities or events. Give concise clinical justifications, not a private reasoning trace.
cases.source: https://casereports.bmj.com/content/19/10/e275187; Exposure and repeated presentations, p-4–p-7; imaging, p-8; treatment and recovery, p-12–p-13; causal limitation, p-17
cases.reference: Fever with new frontal/periorbital swelling and an abscess warrants urgent specialist evaluation rather than reassurance based on modest inflammatory markers. Assess ocular and neurological complications and source control needs. CT without demonstrated extension is not proof that all possible complications are excluded; osteomyelitis is not MRI-confirmed. Pressure-related injury is a hypothesis and sinusitis itself could explain progression. Exact earlier antibiotic sequence is not a scoring target because source descriptions differ.

interview.decision_point: Return with fever and forehead swelling after sinusitis treatment; before operative drainage and microbiology.

cases.title: B07 — Cholestasis with a large liver cyst
cases.facts:
A man in his 70s with known hepatic cysts developed right-upper-quadrant pain, early satiety, anorexia and dark urine. Initial imaging showed an 11.5 cm septated cyst without bile-duct dilatation. Bilirubin was 157 micromol/L, direct bilirubin 111, ALP 451 U/L, AST 114 and ALT 140.
Aspiration yielded benign cytology and some biochemical improvement, but cholestasis persisted. Smooth-muscle antibody was weakly positive. Liver biopsy showed acute-on-chronic cholestatic hepatitis, mild interface change and focal bridging fibrosis, without prominent plasma cells. MRCP showed cyst mass effect but no duct dilatation.
Symptoms recurred with a 14×12 cm cyst, possible internal haemorrhage, bilirubin 115, direct bilirubin 91 and ALP 365. Subsequent surgery, histology and response are not supplied.
cases.task: Audience: a clinician. Use 200–280 words in English. Compare plausible explanations for the cholestasis and explain the limits of the antibody, biopsy and imaging findings. State a proportionate next evaluation and how much causal certainty is justified before intervention. Use only the information supplied at this decision point. Distinguish observed facts, hypotheses and proposed actions. Do not invent results, doses, probabilities or events. Give concise clinical justifications, not a private reasoning trace.
cases.source: https://casereports.bmj.com/content/19/10/e275824; Previous investigations, p-5–p-6; repeat blood tests and imaging, p-7; intervention and outcome, p-10–p-12; interpretation, p-18
cases.reference: Integrate recurrent cyst enlargement, symptoms and cholestatic tests without treating absence of duct dilatation as definitive exclusion of mechanical contribution. Weak antibody positivity and limited interface change do not independently establish autoimmune hepatitis. Compression is a plausible mechanism but not demonstrated with certainty. Review imaging/pathology and specialist management options; do not cite an undisclosed postoperative response.

interview.decision_point: Recurrent symptoms and enlargement of a hepatic cyst, before fenestration or subsequent biochemical recovery.

cases.title: B08 — Severe gastrointestinal bleeding after neurosurgery
cases.facts:
An adolescent boy received ketorolac in hospital after revision posterior-fossa surgery and was prescribed ibuprofen 400 mg as needed every six hours for about a week. No excess use is reported.
On postoperative day 9 he had epigastric pain and constipation without haematemesis or melaena. By day 14 he developed melaena, dizziness and syncope, with blood pressure 90/47 mm Hg and pulse 128/min, requiring intensive care.
Haemoglobin was initially recorded as 92 g/L and later as 5.2 g/dL; the precise interval between these measurements is not supplied. Platelets were 368×10^9/L, INR 1.0 and aPTT 28 s.
Multiphasic CT showed duodenitis, possible contained ulcer perforation and blood in the stomach, but no active bleeding or pseudoaneurysm. Endoscopy found a posterior duodenal-bulb clot that could not be removed and a separate 5 mm clean-based ulcer. Subsequent angiography is not supplied.
cases.task: Audience: a clinician. Use 200–280 words in English. Identify the immediate priorities for ongoing gastrointestinal bleeding. Explain why the CT and endoscopy do not settle the source, discuss relevant medication exposure without claiming it is proved causal, and state the next specialist actions. Avoid procedural or drug dosing instructions. Use only the information supplied at this decision point. Distinguish observed facts, hypotheses and proposed actions. Do not invent results, doses, probabilities or events. Give concise clinical justifications, not a private reasoning trace.
cases.source: https://casereports.bmj.com/content/19/10/e273952; History and deterioration, p-4–p-5; CT and endoscopic findings, p-19–p-20; resuscitation and angiography, p-26–p-28; causal uncertainty, p-31
cases.reference: Shock with severe gastrointestinal blood loss requires immediate resuscitation and specialist escalation. A negative active-bleeding CT is time-limited, and an adherent clot prevents complete assessment of the ulcer bed. Consider ongoing or intermittent bleeding and a vascular source without requiring the hidden angiographic diagnosis. NSAID exposure is relevant but does not prove the full ulcer/pseudoaneurysm mechanism. Do not calculate an exact haemoglobin fall over an invented interval.

interview.decision_point: Postoperative day 14, after shock, CT and limited endoscopy, before angiography.

cases.title: B09 — New cranial nerve symptoms in a patient with EGPA
cases.facts:
A man in his 60s has longstanding asthma, nasal polyps, sinus disease and previous eosinophilia up to 3.8×10^9/L. ANCA was negative and earlier biopsies did not show vasculitis. A clinical diagnosis of eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis had been made. Mepolizumab controlled symptoms for five years; he stopped it two years ago.
Asthma and sinus symptoms returned over the past year. He developed right facial pain seven months ago, steroid-responsive bilateral facial weakness five months ago and painful right visual loss three months ago. Vision improved after prednisone and doxycycline, without establishing which intervention explained it.
Following a prednisone reduction from 30 to 20 mg, right V2 pain and sensory loss persisted. An outside MRI reading emphasised small-vessel and sinus changes; institutional review describes multifocal dural enhancement. Later symptoms, cardiac tests and treatment response are not supplied.
cases.task: Audience: a clinician. Use 200–280 words in English. Synthesise the evolving neurological problem and compare up to three explanations. Explain how the historical disease label, negative tests, steroid response and revised imaging should influence a provisional assessment and urgent further review. Use only the information supplied at this decision point. Distinguish observed facts, hypotheses and proposed actions. Do not invent results, doses, probabilities or events. Give concise clinical justifications, not a private reasoning trace.
cases.source: https://casereports.bmj.com/content/19/10/e275382; Historical disease and treatment, p-4; new symptoms and imaging review, p-5–p-7; later progression and response, p-9–p-12
cases.reference: The cranial symptoms and dural enhancement warrant neurological/ophthalmological reassessment in the context of systemic inflammatory disease. Historical clinical EGPA and steroid response raise suspicion but do not prove the cause of every new lesion. Preserve infectious, neoplastic and other inflammatory alternatives where appropriate. Distinguish the earlier MRI interpretation from the later reread. Visual deterioration is important; no hidden cardiac result should be demanded.

interview.decision_point: After recurrent cranial symptoms and institutional MRI review, before later cardiac involvement and treatment response.

cases.title: B10 — Late pain in prosthetic knees after bladder treatment
cases.facts:
A man in his late 60s had bilateral knee replacements. Nineteen months later he received one intravesical BCG instillation for bladder cancer, followed by mitomycin. Sixteen months after BCG he developed bilateral knee pain, worse on the left, without fever, chills or weight loss. Examination showed mild warmth and effusions, with stable observations.
ESR was 32 mm/hour, CRP 1.6 mg/L and procalcitonin 0.1 ng/mL, with normal blood count and liver tests. Initial imaging did not demonstrate loosening or clear infection.
Right-knee aspirate Gram stain and routine cultures were negative. Synovial cell counts and chemistry are unavailable in the selected report. Acid-fast staining was negative, but delayed mycobacterial culture subsequently grew M. tuberculosis complex. Strain identification and later outcomes are withheld.
cases.task: Audience: a clinician. Use 200–280 words in English. Explain the relevant exposure-to-symptom sequence and reconcile the microbiology results. State what further identification and specialist assessment are needed before a management decision. Do not recommend a universal surgical or antimicrobial regimen. Use only the information supplied at this decision point. Distinguish observed facts, hypotheses and proposed actions. Do not invent results, doses, probabilities or events. Give concise clinical justifications, not a private reasoning trace.
cases.source: https://casereports.bmj.com/content/19/10/e270822; History, p-6–p-7; investigations and unavailable measurements, p-8–p-11; management rationale, p-17–p-21; follow-up, p-22–p-26
cases.reference: Prior intravesical BCG is relevant to delayed possible prosthetic-joint infection. Negative routine cultures and AFB stain do not negate a subsequent positive mycobacterial culture. Preserve the distinction between M. tuberculosis complex and a confirmed BCG strain until typing is supplied. Unavailable aspirate counts are not normal or a failure by the model. Specialist treatment and operative choices depend on further evidence; the later selected non-operative success is not a universal standard.

interview.decision_point: After a delayed mycobacterial culture grows M. tuberculosis complex, before strain identification and long-term management.

cases.title: B11 — Persistent vomiting after initially denying medication use
cases.facts:
A woman in her mid-20s has five days of nausea and vomiting, poor intake and initially reported loose stools. Two previous visits led to intravenous fluids and antiemetics. She initially denied medicines, cannabis, other drugs, recent travel and infectious contacts.
Observations are stable and abdominal tenderness is mild without peritonism. Blood count, renal function, electrolytes, liver tests, lipase, glucose and CRP are normal. Urine testing, abdominal ultrasound and brain MRI have not explained the illness.
A repeated, non-judgemental exposure history reveals four weekly injections sold as “retatrutide” by a non-medical wellness coach. The reported amounts were 6, 8, 10 and 12 units on a U-100 syringe (0.06–0.12 mL). Concentration, milligram dose, product purity and actual identity are unknown. Symptoms began after the third injection and worsened after the fourth, given 2–4 days before presentation. She did not regard these as medication.
cases.task: Audience: a clinician. Use 200–280 words in English. Provide a provisional assessment and explain the value of the revised history. State a safe clinical review plan and what can be inferred about the exposure. Do not convert syringe units into an invented milligram dose or assume the product label verifies its contents. Use only the information supplied at this decision point. Distinguish observed facts, hypotheses and proposed actions. Do not invent results, doses, probabilities or events. Give concise clinical justifications, not a private reasoning trace.
cases.source: https://casereports.bmj.com/content/19/10/e276106; Presentation and initial history, p-9–p-12; disclosure and unknown product details, p-13–p-16; causal assessment, p-24; outcome, p-28
cases.reference: Unregulated exposure temporally associated with symptoms is a plausible contributor, not a verified compound-specific diagnosis. A negative initial medication history may reflect category misunderstanding rather than deception. Clarify formulation, other exposures, hydration and ongoing symptoms without inventing product concentration. Assess symptomatic safety and arrange appropriate clinical review. The source is inconsistent about diarrhoea, so absence of diarrhoea is not a required discriminator.

interview.decision_point: After disclosure of wellness injections, before stopping them or observing recovery.

cases.title: B12 — Recurrent dangerous arrhythmias and abnormal thyroid tests
cases.facts:
A man in his mid-60s has ischaemic cardiomyopathy, prior bypass surgery, ejection fraction 33%, a left-ventricular thrombus treated with warfarin and a CRT-defibrillator. Recurrent ventricular tachycardia required previous ablations. Amiodarone and mexiletine began two years ago, when TSH was 0.91 mIU/L.
He now has recurrent ventricular tachycardia and device therapies. TSH is below 0.01, free T4 36.1 pmol/L and free T3 7.3 pmol/L. TSH-receptor antibody is weakly positive at 1.5; thyroid-peroxidase antibody is negative.
Technetium uptake is nearly absent, but the scan was performed after one week of carbimazole 20 mg daily. Ultrasound reports no nodules and no increased vascularity. Subsequent deterioration, rescue therapy and outcomes are not supplied.
cases.task: Audience: a clinician. Use 200–280 words in English. Synthesise the cardiac and thyroid problem, compare plausible thyroid mechanisms and explain the limits of subtype classification. State immediate multidisciplinary priorities without providing a fixed treatment or withdrawal regimen. Use only the information supplied at this decision point. Distinguish observed facts, hypotheses and proposed actions. Do not invent results, doses, probabilities or events. Give concise clinical justifications, not a private reasoning trace.
cases.source: https://casereports.bmj.com/content/19/10/e274623; History and initial findings, p-6–p-8; deterioration, p-11–p-12; subtype uncertainty, p-18; interventions and outcome, p-23–p-28
cases.reference: Thyrotoxicosis during amiodarone therapy is clinically important in a patient with recurrent ventricular arrhythmia and impaired cardiac function. Thyroid subtype cannot be established solely from weak antibody positivity or low uptake after treatment; a mixed or uncertain mechanism is possible. Urgent cardiology/endocrinology review should weigh arrhythmia control and thyroid treatment together. Do not simply demand abrupt withdrawal of a clinically necessary antiarrhythmic or prescribe the later rescue sequence. The source caption/ultrasound discrepancy about nodules is not a scoring key.

interview.decision_point: Initial thyrotoxicosis assessment during recurrent ventricular tachycardia, before later arrest or rescue interventions.

cases.title: B13 — New liver lesions during lymphoma treatment
cases.facts:
A man in his 80s previously had follicular lymphoma followed by high-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC, BCL2 and BCL6 alterations and marrow involvement. He received six cycles of R-mini-CHOP.
Subsequent imaging showed a mixed response with new liver lesions; earlier clavicular and periportal samples were negative for lymphoma. The liver biopsy expressed histiocytic/dendritic markers rather than B-cell markers. MYC and BCL2 abnormalities overlapped with earlier material.
Clonality testing on the original follicular lymphoma was not completed. The material does not securely establish one precise histiocytic/dendritic subtype. Later therapies, relapse and survival outcomes are not supplied.
cases.task: Audience: a clinician. Use 200–280 words in English. Synthesise the discordant imaging and pathology, distinguish supported findings from lineage or clonal hypotheses, and identify what specialist comparison or further evidence is needed. Do not force a specific rare subtype or claim definitive clonal proof. Use only the information supplied at this decision point. Distinguish observed facts, hypotheses and proposed actions. Do not invent results, doses, probabilities or events. Give concise clinical justifications, not a private reasoning trace.
cases.source: https://casereports.bmj.com/content/19/10/e273164; Presentation, p-4; pathology and molecular findings, p-8–p-13; treatment, sec-5; outcome, sec-6; classification discussion, p-24
cases.reference: New lesions after treatment require tissue-based reassessment rather than automatic attribution to persistent B-cell lymphoma. Morphology/immunophenotype and shared alterations support consideration of lineage change, but absent original clonality testing limits proof. Shared abnormalities do not by themselves settle every classification issue. Explain why expert pathology comparison and appropriate molecular correlation matter; avoid requiring a uniquely named subtype from incomplete material.

interview.decision_point: After a new liver biopsy and comparison testing, before later treatment response and relapse.

cases.title: B14 — Restricted hip movement followed by postoperative kidney injury
cases.facts:
A woman in her late 40s had two years of atraumatic left-hip pain, restricted movement and an iliopsoas mass. There was no relevant trauma, injection, prior surgery, anticoagulant exposure, neurological injury or bleeding history. Excision after unsuccessful conservative management showed mature heterotopic ossification.
On postoperative day 3 she became pale and oliguric, without fever, hypotension, recognised bleeding or sepsis. Haemoglobin is 8.3 g/dL, platelets 41×10^9/L, creatinine 12.6 mg/dL, urea 204 mg/dL and LDH 714 U/L. Schistocytes are present. Bilirubin is 4.4 mg/dL, predominantly conjugated. C3 is low at 40 mg/dL and C4 normal; urine protein:creatinine ratio is 17.3.
ADAMTS13 activity is 62% without inhibitor; PT 12 s, INR 1.0 and aPTT 34.2 s. Cultures are negative. Complement genetic testing and anti-factor-H antibodies are unavailable. Treatment response is not known.
cases.task: Audience: a clinician. Use 200–280 words in English. Synthesise the postoperative renal and haematological emergency, compare key thrombotic-microangiopathy explanations and explain the limits of the available tests. State immediate specialist priorities without asserting a confirmed inherited complement disorder or prescribing a regimen. Use only the information supplied at this decision point. Distinguish observed facts, hypotheses and proposed actions. Do not invent results, doses, probabilities or events. Give concise clinical justifications, not a private reasoning trace.
cases.source: https://casereports.bmj.com/content/19/10/e272969; Presentation, p-6–p-7; postoperative deterioration and tests, p-16–p-17; recovery, p-18–p-22; unavailable testing, p-28
cases.reference: New severe renal impairment, thrombocytopenia and schistocytes require urgent nephrology/haematology assessment for thrombotic microangiopathy and alternatives. Supplied ADAMTS13 and coagulation tests inform the differential but should not be overextended. Low C3 may support further complement assessment without proving a genetic cause; missing genetic/antibody tests are unavailable, not negative. Preserve postoperative chronology and avoid causal certainty that surgery alone established a specific mechanism.

interview.decision_point: Postoperative day 3 with new organ failure and haemolytic findings, before plasma exchange, dialysis response or recovery.

cases.title: B15 — Visual deterioration years after thyroid surgery
cases.facts:
A woman in her late 70s had surgery intended as total thyroidectomy for Graves’ disease 15 years ago. Her levothyroxine requirement declined from 300 to 25 micrograms daily. She developed painful proptosis, diplopia and reduced colour vision over several months.
Initial visual acuity was 0.3 right and 0.2 left; Hertel measurements were 27/25 mm and clinical activity score 3. There was no optic-disc swelling. TSH was below 0.01, free T4 15 pmol/L and T3 2.1 nmol/L; TRAb 80.6 and thyroglobulin 131.1. Imaging demonstrated functioning residual or ectopic thyroid tissue.
Initial orbital CT did not show optic-nerve compression. A history of stroke and atrial fibrillation influenced treatment choices. Following initial specialist treatment, acuity rapidly declined to 0.2/0.05 and colour testing became markedly abnormal. Later decompression and outcomes are not supplied.
cases.task: Audience: a clinician. Use 200–280 words in English. Provide a clinical synthesis and explain how worsening visual function should be weighed against the initial CT findings. State urgent specialist priorities and relevant uncertainty without prescribing a treatment regimen or claiming that one later intervention proved causation. Use only the information supplied at this decision point. Distinguish observed facts, hypotheses and proposed actions. Do not invent results, doses, probabilities or events. Give concise clinical justifications, not a private reasoning trace.
cases.source: https://casereports.bmj.com/content/19/10/e275833; History and eye findings, p-7–p-10; biochemistry and imaging, p-11–p-17; deterioration and intervention, p-18–p-19; follow-up, p-20–p-23
cases.reference: Deteriorating vision and colour function in this context warrant urgent ophthalmic/specialist reassessment even without compression on the earlier CT. Normal circulating hormone values do not exclude important orbital disease. Preserve the difference between intended total surgery and functioning residual tissue. Comorbid risks affect intervention choices; do not treat one pathway as mandatory solely because it was used later, or attribute improvement to one of overlapping treatments.

interview.decision_point: After rapid visual decline during treatment, before orbital decompression or response.

cases.title: B16 — Persistent scrotal inflammation in Crohn’s disease
cases.facts:
A man in his early 50s has 25 years of penetrating ileocolonic Crohn’s disease, previously controlled for three years with infliximab. Enterography 11 months earlier did not show a fistula.
He developed recurrent right testicular pain and swelling. Cultures over the course of repeated procedures grew different organisms, including Peptoniphilus, Bacteroides, Citrobacter, Proteus, E. coli, Klebsiella and Morganella. Epididymal/testicular surgery showed necrotising granulomatous inflammation. Acid-fast and fungal studies and selected PCR tests were negative. Brucella testing was not performed because no risk was identified; Bartonella testing was negative.
Later CT did not show active bowel disease or a fistula and he reported no gastrointestinal symptoms. Fresh cultures were not obtained at one later procedure; previous susceptibility results were used. Inflammation persisted despite prolonged antibiotics. Infliximab was held. Subsequent treatment and response are withheld.
cases.task: Audience: a clinician. Use 200–280 words in English. Synthesise the persistent genitourinary problem, compare infectious and inflammatory explanations and identify what evidence should be revisited before changing treatment. Preserve distinctions between positive, negative and unperformed investigations. Use only the information supplied at this decision point. Distinguish observed facts, hypotheses and proposed actions. Do not invent results, doses, probabilities or events. Give concise clinical justifications, not a private reasoning trace.
cases.source: https://casereports.bmj.com/content/19/10/e270689; History, p-7–p-8; cultures and pathology, p-9–p-20; differential and sampling limitations, p-21–p-22; reassessment and response, p-23–p-24
cases.reference: Persistent inflammation despite antimicrobial and surgical management warrants reassessment, including possible extraintestinal Crohn’s involvement, but positive cultures cannot be rewritten as all-negative or automatically dismissed. Negative selected tests and absent demonstrated fistula do not establish a sterile mechanism. The later lack of fresh cultures is an evidence limitation. Consider infection control, specimen/pathology review and immunosuppression risks jointly; do not assert a proved extraintestinal cause from a hidden response.

interview.decision_point: After repeated positive cultures, surgery and persistent inflammation despite antibiotics, before a new immunomodulator or its response.

cases.title: B17 — New vascular symptoms across decades
cases.facts:
One man has had three vascular presentations at different ages and sites.
In his 40s, tinnitus and temporal headache led to diagnosis of a left transverse/sigmoid dural arteriovenous fistula, type IIa+b with venous reflux. Three embolisations relieved symptoms and subsequent MRI remained clear for about 14 years.
In his 50s, pulsatile scalp symptoms, right-sided weakness/numbness and aphasia accompanied a new superior-sagittal-sinus fistula with multiple feeders. Three further embolisations achieved near-occlusion, with about five years of clear follow-up imaging.
In his 60s he developed right occipital pain, retromastoid tenderness and intermittent tinnitus. Angiography in 2018 showed a right transverse/sigmoid fistula classified as type I. The selected record does not specify a new neurological deficit. Later surveillance and symptom outcomes are not supplied. Reported intervals are approximate and should not be combined into an invented exact timeline.
cases.task: Audience: a clinician. Use 200–280 words in English. Summarise the three episodes in order, distinguish a newly located lesion from simple same-site recurrence and explain which supplied features matter for the current risk and specialist discussion. Do not require a treatment choice solely from the later outcome. Use only the information supplied at this decision point. Distinguish observed facts, hypotheses and proposed actions. Do not invent results, doses, probabilities or events. Give concise clinical justifications, not a private reasoning trace.
cases.source: https://casereports.bmj.com/content/19/10/e271253; Episodes and imaging, p-4–p-9; investigations, p-10; treatment decisions, p-16; follow-up, p-17
cases.reference: This is one patient with sequential lesions, not three independent cases. Preserve left transverse/sigmoid, superior sagittal and right transverse/sigmoid sites and the difference between earlier reflux and the currently reported type I lesion. Current management needs specialist assessment of venous drainage, symptoms and preferences; previous treatment success alone does not dictate intervention now. Use approximate source intervals rather than an artificial exact duration.

interview.decision_point: At the third vascular presentation, after angiography classifies the new lesion but before surveillance outcome.

cases.title: B18 — Parenting concerns at a child’s routine visit
cases.facts:
A parent brings a three-year-old boy because of several months of anxiety/worry, poor sleep, limited eye contact, tantrums and attention-seeking behaviour.
The mother’s parenting questionnaire score is 6. She reports occasional yelling, spanking and threats. The parents remain together, financial circumstances are described as stable, family support is available and no substance use is reported. These background facts do not establish that the child has no safeguarding or developmental needs.
At this visit, the father has not been directly assessed. No later questionnaire scores or improvement are supplied. The questionnaire is a screening tool, not a diagnosis of abuse or of a specific developmental disorder.
cases.task: Audience: a parent or caregiver. Use 200–280 words in English. Write a supportive explanation directly to the parent. Address the child’s difficulties and non-violent ways to respond, propose a practical next step and appropriate follow-up, and explain what further assessment could clarify persistent concerns. Avoid blame, a diagnosis from the screening score alone or a promise that one intervention will cure the behaviour. A clinician-style diagnostic one-liner is not required. Use only the information supplied at this decision point. Distinguish observed facts, hypotheses and proposed actions. Do not invent results, doses, probabilities or events. Give concise clinical justifications, not a private reasoning trace.
cases.source: https://casereports.bmj.com/content/19/10/e274343; Family presentation and follow-up, p-7–p-9; interview findings, sec-3; limitations, p-51; parent interviews, sec-17
cases.reference: Offer clear, non-judgemental, developmentally appropriate advice, avoiding endorsement of physical punishment or threats. Discuss positive, predictable responses and support for caregivers alongside evaluation of sleep, development and persistent concerns where warranted. A questionnaire score is not proof of abuse, and a selected family’s later improvement would not prove programme efficacy. The current task is parent communication, not rare-disease diagnosis or compulsory clinical synthesis.

interview.decision_point: Initial paediatric counselling visit, before the family’s later behaviour scores or outcomes.
interview.synthesis_scope: Parent explanation; clinician-style synthesis is outside scope.

cases.title: B19 — Persistent caesarean-scar pain in preterm pregnancy
cases.facts:
A woman in her late 20s, gravida 3 para 2 with two previous caesarean sections, is transferred at 28+4 weeks because of persistent left-sided scar pain and concern about a scar complication. She is stable without vaginal bleeding or ruptured membranes.
BMI is 35 and she has insulin-treated gestational diabetes, platelets 141×10^9/L and depression treated with sertraline. The fetal heart trace is reactive. Ultrasound estimates fetal weight at 2,500 g, above the 99th centile, with polyhydramnios (deepest vertical pocket 8.4 cm). Placenta is anterior without demonstrated abruption and umbilical-artery Doppler is normal.
Lower-segment thickness is reported as 2.7 mm on the right and 1.2 mm on the left, but imaging is technically limited. MRI shows scar thinning and is inconclusive for torsion, dehiscence or rupture. Later clinical progression, delivery timing and operative findings are not supplied.
cases.task: Audience: a clinician. Use 200–280 words in English. Synthesise the maternal–fetal concern, compare the important possibilities and explain what inconclusive imaging means for risk. State priorities for specialist observation/reassessment without declaring a hidden operative diagnosis or a universal delivery threshold. Use only the information supplied at this decision point. cases.title: B20 — New tumour findings after prolonged imatinib response
cases.facts:
A woman in her late 40s originally presented in 2001 with an approximately 8 cm gastric tumour and liver lesions. Initial metastatic-carcinoma treatment produced stable disease. Pathology review in 2002 showed KIT/CD34 positivity with negative desmin/cytokeratin and established GIST. KIT mutation testing was not performed then.
Imatinib began in 2002 at 400 mg daily, rose to 500 mg in 2004 and returned to 400 mg in 2016 because of renal/anaemia concerns. Renal function later declined to eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m²; contrast CT was stopped from 2021.
After about 20.8 years of control, a distal-oesophageal prominence increased over two to three CT examinations across 1–2 years. In 2023 a 33 mm lesion was biopsied as GIST, with KIT, CD34 and DOG1 positivity. Sequencing found a KIT exon 11 driver and exon 13 V654A alteration associated with resistance. The original specimen was inadequate to verify its mutation. Later treatment and outcomes are not supplied.

cases.title: B21 — Unexpected anatomy during hernia repair
cases.facts:
A man in his 60s has a year of intermittent right-groin discomfort with exertion or standing and a reducible inguinal hernia. He has no previous inguinal operation, trauma, urinary symptoms or testicular pain. The scrotal examination was normal. No preoperative imaging was obtained for the uncomplicated clinical hernia.
During elective open repair, two distinct spermatic-cord structures are unexpectedly identified. Each appears to contain a vas and vascular/neural elements; both are traced towards the testis and through a common internal ring. Later ultrasound and postoperative outcome are not available at this decision point. No assumption should be made that an asymptomatic anatomical variant had to be predicted before the operation.

cases.title: J01 — Fever, purpura and evolving renal findings
cases.facts:
A 65-year-old man with ulcerative colitis treated with mesalamine developed a prolonged illness after a sore throat. For about five weeks he has had fever, night sweats, arthralgia and abdominal symptoms. An earlier admission found inflammatory and liver-test abnormalities, but colonoscopy did not show active colitis. Antibiotics and a short prednisone course did not resolve the illness. A low-level EBV DNA result and positive viral-capsid IgM/IgG had led to a working diagnosis of primary EBV infection.
He later developed palpable purpura on the flanks and upper thighs, purpura on the lower legs, transient scrotal pain, joint pain and leg oedema. Earlier urinalyses were normal; at the new admission urine has 2+ protein, 1+ blood and 5–10 red cells/high-power field, with protein:creatinine ratio 0.99. Creatinine is 0.72 mg/dL, albumin 2.6 g/dL and platelets 505000/microlitre. CT shows small-bowel thickening, surrounding inflammatory change and small-volume ascites. He is febrile but haemodynamically stable and mentally alert.
He lived in West Africa and Southeast Asia more than ten years ago, travelled to Florida seven months ago and cleans a neighbour’s chicken coop. A rapid P. falciparum antigen test is positive, but thick and thin blood smears on two days are negative. Biopsy findings and later response are not supplied.

cases.title: J02 — Persistent daytime sleep episodes despite improved mood
cases.facts:

He falls asleep unintentionally on public transport and while reading, and reports sometimes sleeping for very prolonged periods.
Further history includes brief hand weakness when laughing, visual/tactile experiences while falling asleep and repeated awakening with inability to move. His partner has not reported snoring or apnoea. Several relatives have unspecified sleep disorders. He reports no recent non-prescribed opioid use but has recently used ketamine several times a week and alcohol weekly. Routine testing detects buprenorphine and its metabolite but not other tested opioids, benzodiazepines or stimulants; it does not establish absence of every substance.
BMI is 21 and neurological examination is unremarkable. Selected renal, electrolyte, glucose, liver and iron studies are not explanatory. Thyroid testing is not supplied. There is no polysomnography or multiple-sleep-latency result at this point.

cases.title: J03 — Progressive tremor, gait and cognitive symptoms after an initial head-injury label
cases.facts:
A 59-year-old man in coastal southern Norway developed tremor, headache, night sweats and persistent hiccups after a fall with a blow to the back of the head. He has type 2 diabetes and previous thymoma surgery. An initial MRI was reported as unremarkable. Routine blood tests were not explanatory; the initial working diagnosis was post-concussion syndrome.
Symptoms progressed over months to gait difficulty, falls, memory difficulty, dysphagia, resting tremor, bradykinesia and hypophonia. Dopamine-transporter imaging showed reduced uptake, prompting a Parkinson disease hypothesis, but levodopa did not improve symptoms. He was readmitted with worsening weakness, wasting, brisk reflexes and possible fasciculations. Neurophysiological studies were normal. EEG showed mild encephalopathy, and CSF had 443 white cells/microlitre against a reference below 5, with protein 3.03 g/L.

cases.title: J04 — Recurrent destructive ulcers with systemic inflammatory features
cases.facts:
A man first seen at age 41 has recurrent painful oropharyngeal ulceration causing dysphagia, followed by ulcers of the eyelids, tongue dorsum, lip mucosa and penis. Eyelid inflammation caused scarring and ocular surface complications; it is not described as uveitis. No haematological malignancy was established by marrow, flow, protein, imaging and panel workup. Hilar lymphadenopathy was not found, and broad autoimmune serology was not explanatory.

At thirty minutes she has no light perception and a marked relative afferent pupillary defect. Intraocular pressure is 8 mm Hg; the cornea is clear. She has mild ipsilateral supraorbital headache and no reported migraine or neurological history. Neuroimaging has been ordered, but no result is available.

This is an autopsy-tissue series, not an individual diagnostic vignette. Eight deceased people with SOD1-associated ALS had received intrathecal tofersen. Tissue concentrations were examined against dosing histories and pharmacokinetic predictions.
In three recently treated donors, lumbar spinal-cord SOD1 mRNA/protein reductions were reported in the range 45%–84%, relative to tofersen-naive tissue samples. The size and matching of that comparison cohort are not specified in this packet. Residual motor neurons contained drug-related signal; misfolded SOD1 inclusions remained detectable. cases.title: SR03 — Recovery before and after rescue immunotherapy
cases.facts:
A retrospective multicentre series records 18 treated attacks in 17 people with MOGAD or AQP4-positive NMOSD. IL-6 receptor blockade began within one month of attack nadir. Thirteen attacks were treated as acute escalation after inadequate earlier therapy; five represented early initiation of maintenance treatment.
The authors report an EDSS improvement before IL-6 blockade, from a nadir median of 5.0 to a pre-blockade median of 3.5 (P=.001), and a further decrease to 2.0 at three months (P=.03 versus pre-blockade). These are the reported comparison summaries; the packet does not establish the participant subset for every paired comparison. There is no concurrent untreated control group. Earlier corticosteroids/plasma exchange and spontaneous recovery can affect the course.
cases.task: Audience: a clinician. Use 180–240 words in English. Explain what the sequence supports and what it leaves unresolved about an acute rescue effect. Address attacks versus patients, the two treatment intentions, the improvement already present before blockade, and why the reported P values do not alone identify a causal effect. Give brief evidence-based justifications, not a private reasoning trace. Do not invent unreported findings, ages, test results or outcomes. Do not prescribe a dose or claim that an unreported result is normal.
cases.source: https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/2850382; Methods; Results paragraphs on 18 attacks / 17 patients, escalation versus maintenance intent, and pre/post-treatment EDSS.
cases.reference: Do not count 18 attacks as 18 independent patients. Escalation and early-maintenance intentions differ. Improvement preceding blockade must not be attributed to blockade. Subsequent change is an association in a selected uncontrolled series, with prior therapy, natural recovery and subset uncertainty. Statistical significance is not a randomised causal contrast. Do not convert changes in an ordinal EDSS median into a validated percentage recovery.

cases.title: SR05 — Progressive language-led impairment after earlier haemorrhage

A man first developed difficulty organising appointments at age 47. At 49 he had a right parieto-occipital intracerebral haemorrhage, then attributed to hypertension; he recovered physically but required a live-in carer.
By 54, disorientation and loss of recent-event recall had progressed. At approximately 55, speech remained fluent and grammatical, but word retrieval and sentence repetition were markedly impaired; comprehension was relatively preserved. Navigation and dressing also became difficult. He received cadaveric pituitary-derived growth hormone during childhood, including 1974–1985. cases.facts:
A retrospective uncontrolled series treated 33 people with chemotherapy- or radiation-associated skin toxicity using high-dose oral vitamin D. Thirty also received concurrent supportive therapy.
During the reported 10-day interval, 26 of 30 people with symptom data reported relief. Anticancer treatment continued without interruption in 24 of all 33. No treatment-related adverse events were reported. Post-treatment laboratory information was inconsistently available; post-treatment vitamin D levels were measured in 13. The packet supplies neither an untreated group nor patient-level pairing for every outcome.

cases.title: SR08 — Clinical shrinkage versus pathological response
cases.facts:
A prospective uncontrolled series enrolled 15 people with advanced cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck awaiting surgery. All received neoadjuvant capecitabine.
Ten of 15 had clinical tumour reduction. Twelve underwent surgery; five of those twelve had a complete pathological response and seven of twelve were downstaged. Two people with apparent complete clinical lesion resolution chose radiotherapy instead of surgery; another did not proceed to surgery after progression. No grade 3 or higher treatment-related toxicity was reported. There was no comparator group, and follow-up for durability was short.

Explain why clinical disappearance, pathological response and durable cure are different claims. State what can and cannot be concluded about comparative efficacy and safety. Give brief evidence-based justifications, not a private reasoning trace. Do not invent unreported findings, ages, test results or outcomes. Do not prescribe a dose or claim that an unreported result is normal.
